name: Sojourner (Mars Pathfinder rover)

destinations.note: Landed with the Pathfinder lander inside airbags in Ares Vallis.

dateNotes: September 27, 1997 is the last successful data transmission from the lander, which Sojourner relied on to reach Earth. Other sources mention a final signal on October 7, 1997.
Mission end: secondary sources give a farewell announcement on November 4, 1997 and a formal end on March 10, 1998. We could not confirm the date on NASA's page, so the field is empty.

status.text: Silent on the surface of Mars since 1997

finalFate: Sojourner remained on the surface near the lander in Ares Vallis. Its present condition is unknown, and it cannot be assumed to be intact.

location.description: Ares Vallis in the Chryse Planitia region of Mars, near the Pathfinder lander.

instruments.name: Alpha Proton X-ray Spectrometer (APXS)
instruments.role: Identified the chemical elements in rocks and soil.

instruments.name: Rover cameras (two front, one rear)
instruments.role: For driving and close-up pictures of rocks.

primary.title: A tool that knows what a rock is made of
primary.howItWorks: Sojourner held a small instrument against a rock for hours. It measured the rays bouncing back from the rock.
primary.knowledge: Scientists learned that the rocks there were not all the same.

secondary.title: The APXS: how do you measure a rock's elements?
secondary.howItWorks: A small radioactive source bombards the rock surface with alpha particles; the instrument then measures the energies of returning X-rays, protons and alpha particles. Each element has a characteristic energy signature, so relative abundances can be calculated.
secondary.knowledge: The spectrometer measures only the surface it touches, so dust stuck to a rock can change the reading — as happened with the rock 'Yogi'.

engineeringChallenge.challenge: Land on Mars cheaply without a complex landing system, and run a very small rover on limited power.
engineeringChallenge.solution: Airbags that inflated seconds before impact, letting the lander bounce and settle, and having Sojourner talk to Earth through the lander instead of carrying its own Earth radio.

discoveries.text: The APXS reading of the rock 'Barnacle Bill' showed more silica than the expected basalt, closer to andesite.
The first reading of 'Yogi' looked basalt-like, but after correcting for dust its composition was close to Barnacle Bill's.
Images are consistent with Ares Vallis having been the site of a massive flood roughly one to three billion years ago.
The mission proved a small rover can work and move on Mars, and that airbag landings are possible.

timeline.text: Pathfinder lands with airbags in Ares Vallis.
Sojourner rolls down the ramp onto Mars (U.S. time).
Last data transmission from the lander; Sojourner loses its link to Earth.

chapters.text: I am Sojourner, a small rover about the size of a microwave oven. I reached Mars in 1997 with the Pathfinder lander.
I was sent to test a new idea: can a little cart drive around on Mars and check its rocks?
We landed inside big airbags that bounced on the ground like a ball. Then I rolled down a ramp, moved on six wheels, and sent my pictures through the lander.
My special tool showed what rocks were made of. They were different from each other, and the place may once have had a huge flood.
I was planned to work for one week, but I worked for almost three months! Then the lander stopped talking, so I went quiet too. I am still there on Mars.

glossary.meaning: Big bags full of gas that protect a spacecraft when it hits the ground.
A huge amount of water covering and rushing over the land.

chapters.text: I am Sojourner, a six-wheeled rover of about 11 kilograms, part of Mars Pathfinder in NASA's low-cost Discovery program. We launched on December 4, 1996, and landed on July 4, 1997, in Ares Vallis. The lander was later named the Carl Sagan Memorial Station.

My main job was technical: prove that a small rover could drive and work on Mars. Science was a bonus — analyzing rocks on a plain thought to be shaped by ancient floods. Ares Vallis was chosen because it was fairly safe for landing and full of varied rocks.

Airbags inflated seconds before impact, so the lander bounced across the surface and then came to rest. I did not talk to Earth directly; I sent my data to the lander, which relayed it. That design saved mass and power, but it tied my fate to the lander's.

I placed my APXS on rocks to measure their elements. 'Barnacle Bill' looked richer in silica than the expected basalt. 'Yogi' looked different, but dust stuck to it affected the reading; once corrected, it was closer to Barnacle Bill. The lesson: understand your sources of error before interpreting.

I was planned for seven Martian days; I worked for 83 and drove about 100 meters. The lander's last data arrived on September 27, 1997, and my link to Earth was gone. I stayed near the lander, and nobody knows my condition today.

glossary.meaning: A Martian day, slightly longer than an Earth day (about 24 hours 37 minutes).
Silicon dioxide, a main ingredient of many rocks and of sand.

questions.q: How long was Sojourner planned to work?
questions.explanation: It was planned for one week, but it worked for almost three months. Great remembering!

questions.q: How did Sojourner's messages reach Earth?
options: Directly through a big antenna on the rover
questions.explanation: Sojourner was small, so it sent messages to the lander, and the lander sent them to Earth.

secondaryActivity.title: Dust on a rock: how does it change the reading?
secondaryActivity.instructions: Study the simplified summary of APXS readings, then answer.
secondaryActivity.dataNote: A simplified qualitative summary of Mars Pathfinder preliminary results from NASA's NSSDC archive. Detailed numbers are not shown here.

rows: Close to Viking landing-site soils, with differences

task.q: Why did the interpretation of 'Yogi' change?
options: The measurement included dust stuck to its surface; removing that effect changed the result
task.explanation: The spectrometer measures the layer it touches. If dust covers it, the reading is a mix of rock and dust, so scientists corrected it with a mixing model before interpreting.

questions.q: What was the engineering trade-off of relaying Sojourner's data through the lander?
options: Saving mass and power in exchange for total dependence on the lander
More speed in exchange for fewer cameras
questions.explanation: A smart choice for a tiny rover — but when the lander stopped, Sojourner fell silent too.

options: Absorb the shock of hitting the surface
questions.explanation: The lander bounced inside the airbags several times before stopping, which protected it from the impact.

questions.q: 'Ares Vallis was the site of a massive ancient flood.' This statement is…
options: An interpretation based on images and comparison with earlier data
A direct measurement of flowing water today
Information from a message Sojourner sent
questions.explanation: No flowing water was observed; the landforms and rocks are consistent with an ancient flood, which is an interpretation.
